newsitem.title: CROATIA: FEATURE - Ex-rebel Serbs to vote in Croatian elections.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Ex-rebel Serbs to vote in Croatian elections.

text.p: Independent Croatia holds its first peacetime elections on Sunday with many eyes focused on former rebel Serbs opting for ballots over bullets.

The voting for regional councils and the upper House of Counties will include the Serb enclave of Eastern Slavonia, launching its "reintegration" with the rest of the country after a transitional postwar period as a United Nations protectorate.

Analysts say the elections will also provide an important mid-term reading on the fortunes of President Franjo Tudjman's conservative nationalist HDZ party, which has lost popularity but been sustained by opposition disunity.

An HDZ aura of omnipotence, acquired by leading Croatia in a successful war for independence from Serbian-led Yugoslavia in 1991, dimmed in 1995 when its majority in parliament was slashed to a minimum in elections.

Tudjman called the elections after army victories over rebel minority Serbs, hoping that patriotic fervour stirred by battlefield glory would hand the HDZ a two-thirds majority solidifying his authoritarian rule.
The last local elections, in February 1993, were also held on the heels of military gains against the Serbs and yielded resounding HDZ victories in all but two of 21 counties.

But by 1995, many voters were less euphoric about military triumphs than angered by corruption and profiteering by HDZ figures and associates while Croatia's middle class was laid low by war-related inflation and uneven economic reforms.
OPPOSITION HOPING FOR REGIONAL GAINS
The next parliamentary elections will not be held until 1999. But opposition parties are hoping to make inroads into power on Sunday by winning a greater share of regional governments.

In Eastern Slavonia, Serbs were expected to vote en masse for a Serb rights party bloc formed at the last minute after local leaders were told by ex-patron Serbia to abandon dreams of autonomy and obey a United Nations timetable for rejoining Croatia.
Vojislav Stanimirovic, a bearded psychiatrist and relative political moderate, who heads the Serb bloc (SDSS), has negotiated key normalisation pacts with the Croatian authorities.
He has urged his people to turn out in large numbers to maximise their chances of holding Croatia to promises of extensive minority rights after the U.N. leaves.
"Most of the people want to stay. They have little choice since they have nowhere else to go. Serbia cannot help us much anymore, economically or otherwise," he said.

U.N. sources said the Serbs could carry 10-12 of Eastern Slavonia's 30 municipalities. The rest would have Croatian majority councils, elected with the absentee votes of Croat war refugees who will resettle the enclave after reintegration.
DECLINE IN HDZ POPULARITY

Elsewhere, polls show that a combination of the four main opposition parties would oust the HDZ in most cities, including the capital Zagreb which boasts a quarter of Croatia's population and almost half its productive economy.
HDZ popularity has dropped to between 20 and 35 percent in most areas of this republic of 4.7 million people. The HDZ's huge House of Counties majority is almost sure to dwindle.

Despite similar platforms, rival parties did not form uniform and big enough blocs to challenge the HDZ head-on across Croatia, as Serbia's Together coalition did successfully against the Socialists of President Slobodan Milosevic.

Croatian opposition alliances varied between districts, leaving Sunday's outcome unclear in all but liberal Istria, an opposition bastion on the Adriatic coast that has long resisted the centralist, nationalist tilt of Zagreb.
"The opposition behaves like it wants the HDZ to stay in power," remarked the independent weekly Globus.

Opposition solidarity was also undermined by the fact that the main players differ little from the HDZ on fundamental issues such as privatisation, a strong army and national pride. All have a wary approach to relations with Serbia.
HDZ MOVES TO BOOST ITS POSITION
The HDZ tailored its campaign to counter accusations that it is aloof, callous, corrupt and isolated by a sceptical West.

There was a pre-election blitz of HDZ ministerial visits to major foreign countries and ribbon-cutting ceremonies at home to open new roads, factories and so on, coupled with pledges to raise meagre pensions and wages and crack down on graft.

World Bank and IMF packages to spur postwar reconstruction and development have been announced. Croatia has also just obtained its first sovereign credit rating, a reward for overall economic stability and low inflation since 1994.

State television, the sole source of news for most Croats, has lavished coverage on events favourable to the HDZ, especially public walkabouts by a reinvigorated Tudjman, the only truly popular and charismatic politician in Croatia.

Some diplomats expected an inconclusive election outcome that might force the HDZ into coalitions. Opposition newspapers say the HDZ would not be above resorting to legal manoeuvres or fraud to retain power alone.

A seven-party opposition bloc outpolled the HDZ in 1995 elections for Zagreb's regional government but fell apart after Tudjman refused to approve a non-HDZ mayoralty, exercising a presidential "national security" veto.
Tudjman, expected to win summer presidential elections easily, said recently he would respect any verdict by voters.

Some analysts believe the HDZ would now think twice about denying opposition victories to avoid possible mass protests like those which forced Serbia's Socialists to admit defeat in municipal elections last November.

But others say a protest movement in Croatia is improbable now because the opposition would fear being accused by the HDZ of causing turmoil ruinous for the approaching tourist season, a crucial foreign-exchange earner.
